title: D-penicillamine in Primary Biliary Cholangitis
text:
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic, progressive cholestatic liver disease. The Mayo Clinic trial randomised patients to D-penicillamine, an immunomodulator, or placebo, with the working hypothesis that slowing disease progression would delay death or the need for liver transplantation. The public dataset (survival::pbc) contains laboratory markers, clinical signs, and follow-up times for 418 patients.
Of these, 106 were not randomised (an observational follow-up group) and are excluded from every analysis below. The analysis cohort is therefore 312 randomised patients.
The endpoint variable is worth pausing on. The raw status field has three levels:

0 censored,
1 transplant,
2 death.

Two analyses are possible from this one field, and they answer different questions. Collapsing transplant and death into a single “composite” event asks whether treatment delays the first unfavourable event of any kind. Keeping them apart asks whether treatment changes the risk of death specifically, treating transplant as a competing event that removes a patient from the risk set for death. Because a transplant is not obviously a bad outcome, the two analyses can disagree in direction, and that disagreement is itself the interesting finding. This report runs both.

5.1 Checking the proportional hazards assumption
A Cox model reports one hazard ratio per covariate, which is only meaningful if that ratio is constant over follow-up. The Schoenfeld residual test checks this assumption; a significant p-value means the HR drifts over time and should not be reported as a single number.


Show the code
ph_linear <- ph_test(fit_cox_multi_linear(prepare_s1()))
ph_linear


           chisq df      p
trt      0.00896  1 0.9246
age      3.48305  1 0.0620
bili     7.69013  1 0.0056
protime  5.35633  1 0.0206
GLOBAL  17.57699  4 0.0015




Show the code
ph_plot(ph_linear, base_size = 11)








Figure 3: Schoenfeld residuals for the linear-covariate model. A non-horizontal trend indicates the hazard ratio changes over time.

Figure 5: Schoenfeld residuals for the linear-covariate model. A non-horizontal trend indicates the hazard ratio changes over time.











Figure 6: Schoenfeld residuals for the linear-covariate model. A non-horizontal trend indicates the hazard ratio changes over time.





The test flags prothrombin time as violating the assumption. Because bilirubin and prothrombin time are strictly positive and act multiplicatively on the hazard, the standard remedy is to model them on the log scale.


Show the code
# Build the log-transformed variant inside the analysis so the transformation
# is visible in the report rather than buried in a helper.
s1_log <- prepare_s1() |>
  mutate(log_bili = log(bili), log_protime = log(protime)) |>
  add_protime_cat()

cox_log <- coxph(
  Surv(time, status) ~ trt + age + log(bili) + log(protime),
  data = s1_log
)
ph_test(cox_log)


              chisq df     p
trt          0.0226  1 0.880
age          2.9758  1 0.085
log(bili)    0.2619  1 0.609
log(protime) 5.6917  1 0.017
GLOBAL       8.2763  4 0.082


Log-transforming bilirubin resolves its violation, but prothrombin time still fails. When a covariate cannot be made to satisfy proportional hazards, the correct move is to stratify on it rather than force a single HR: the model then estimates the treatment effect within strata of prothrombin time and makes no assumption about its shape over time.
The cost is that a stratified Cox model cannot estimate an HR for the stratification variable itself. Since prothrombin time is a strong prognostic marker but not our exposure of interest, this is an acceptable trade.


Show the code
s1_strat <- add_protime_cat(prepare_s1())
cox_strat <- fit_cox_multi_stratified(s1_strat)
ph_strat  <- ph_test(cox_strat)

format_cox_table(
  cox_strat,
  caption = "Multivariable Cox regression, stratified by prolonged prothrombin time"
) |> as_gt()

The stratification clears the remaining violation, and the substantive conclusion is unchanged: the treatment HR stays close to 1 and non-significant, while age and log-bilirubin carry the prognostic signal.

title: D-penicillamine in Primary Biliary Cholangitis
text:
7.1 Limitations
The trial is small and the follow-up is long, so the covariate-adjusted estimates carry wide confidence intervals. Prothrombin time is dichotomised at the upper limit of normal (11 s) to enable stratification; this cut point is clinically motivated but does not use the full information in the marker, and a continuous spline or time-varying coefficient would be a reasonable extension. Finally, this is a re-analysis of a public dataset for methodological illustration, not a new clinical claim.
